reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Infarction in the territory of the single anterior spinal artery affects the ventral two-thirds of the cord, producing acute para- or tetraplegia below the level of the lesion

There is a dissociated sensory loss, with loss of pain and temperature from spinothalamic tract involvement but relative preservation of proprioception, vibration and fine touch because the dorsal columns are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries
Autonomic disturbance is prominent, with early urinary retention, bowel dysfunction and, in high lesions, neurogenic hypotension
The initial phase is one of spinal shock with flaccid, areflexic weakness, which later evolves into spasticity and hyperreflexia
The mid-thoracic cord is a watershed zone and is particularly vulnerable to hypoperfusion

Common causes include aortic surgery, dissection or aneurysm, systemic hypotension, atheroembolism, vasculitis and fibrocartilaginous embolism, while a young patient may have an underlying thrombophilia
The lower cord depends heavily on the artery of Adamkiewicz, usually arising on the left between the ninth thoracic and second lumbar segments
Early MRI may be normal, so a high index of suspicion and repeat diffusion-weighted imaging are needed to confirm cord infarction
reference.pathophysiology: The anterior spinal artery is a single midline vessel that supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the anterior horns, the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and the intermediolateral autonomic columns; it is reinforced only intermittently by radicular feeders, the largest being the artery of Adamkiewicz. Occlusion or critical hypoperfusion of this vessel, or of its feeders, causes ischaemic infarction of the ventral cord while sparing the dorsal columns, which derive their blood supply from the paired posterior spinal arteries. The sparse segmental reinforcement leaves watershed regions, especially in the mid-thoracic cord, most susceptible to global hypotension, and the resulting infarct produces the characteristic combination of motor paralysis, dissociated sensory loss and autonomic failure.
additionalDifferentials: Acute compressive myelopathy from disc, tumour or epidural haematoma
Transverse myelitis and other inflammatory myelopathies
Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula with venous congestion
Guillain-Barre syndrome in the early flaccid phase
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
additionalInvestigations: Urgent MRI of the spinal cord with diffusion-weighted imaging showing anterior T2 hyperintensity, sometimes with an owl-eye pattern and restricted diffusion
CT or MR angiography of the aorta to identify dissection, aneurysm or atheromatous disease
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude an inflammatory or infective myelopathy
Echocardiography and cardiac rhythm assessment to seek an embolic source
Vasculitis and autoimmune screen where an inflammatory arteriopathy is considered
Thrombophilia evaluation in younger patients without an obvious vascular cause
redFlags: Acute paraplegia or tetraplegia with a clear sensory level demanding emergency evaluation
Tearing chest or back pain suggesting aortic dissection as the underlying cause
Haemodynamic instability that may perpetuate cord ischaemia
Acute urinary retention indicating autonomic involvement
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally guarded, and many patients are left with substantial permanent motor and autonomic deficits. A complete deficit at onset and an extensive infarct on imaging predict a poorer outcome, whereas incomplete syndromes may recover partially.
pitfalls: Mistaking the early flaccid, areflexic phase for Guillain-Barre syndrome
Missing an underlying aortic dissection as the cause of cord ischaemia
Assuming that preserved proprioception excludes a significant cord lesion
Being falsely reassured by an early normal MRI before diffusion changes have appeared
Overlooking correctable hypotension that is prolonging watershed ischaemia
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying vascular cause urgently — surgical or endovascular repair of aortic dissection or aneurysm, and correct precipitating systemic hypotension to restore cord perfusion
Optimise spinal cord perfusion with blood-pressure augmentation and, in the peri-aortic-surgery setting, cerebrospinal fluid drainage
Direct antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy by the underlying mechanism (atheroembolism, cardioembolic source or thrombophilia)
Supportive care of the flaccid spinal-shock phase: urinary catheterisation for retention, a bowel regimen, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and pressure-area skin care
Manage evolving spasticity with antispasticity agents such as baclofen alongside physiotherapy, and treat neuropathic pain
Early multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and spinal specialists to maximise functional recovery
Investigate thrombophilia in younger patients and involve haematology where an inherited prothrombotic disorder is confirmed
